overview: This file documents the transformation of Japanese labor and economic policy between 1930 and 1939, from early wage adjustments and limited statutory protections for miners, women, and minors to the comprehensive regulation of a wartime command economy. Consular and Embassy reports provide detailed regional and national evidence on wages, employment, hours, benefits, commodity prices, and living costs in Japan and colonial Taiwan, while highlighting the difficulty of comparing basic wages when compensation also included bonuses, housing, food, pensions, and medical care. The closing despatch and translated ordinances reveal how inflation, government borrowing problems, hoarding, and speculation during the war in China prompted controls over prices, wages, corporate remuneration, rents, and electric power under the National General Mobilization Law.
interest: Shift from labor regulation to wartime control, via consular wage surveys and 1939 ordinances on prices, rents, wages and power.
